claim: In plants, selfish genetic elements, including retrotransposons and DNA viruses, are transcriptionally silenced by RNA-directed DNA methylation.
source: In plants, selfish genetic elements, including retrotransposons and DNA viruses, are transcriptionally silenced by RNA-directed DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in plant biology supported by the citation context of the manuscript and general scientific knowledge.

claim: siRNAs guiding RNA-directed DNA methylation are cut by DICER-LIKE 3 (DCL3) from double-stranded precursors of ~30 bp.
source: Guiding the process are short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) cut by DICER-LIKE 3 (DCL3) from double-stranded precursors of ~30 bp that are synthesized by NUCLEAR RNA POLYMERASE IV (Pol IV) and RNA-DEPENDENT RNA POLYMERASE 2 (RDR2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Double-stranded siRNA precursors are synthesized by NUCLEAR RNA POLYMERASE IV (Pol IV) and RNA-DEPENDENT RNA POLYMERASE 2 (RDR2).
source: Guiding the process are short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) cut by DICER-LIKE 3 (DCL3) from double-stranded precursors of ~30 bp that are synthesized by NUCLEAR RNA POLYMERASE IV (Pol IV) and RNA-DEPENDENT RNA POLYMERASE 2 (RDR2).
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and experimental data.

claim: Pol IV's choice of initiating nucleotide influences which precursor end is diced by DCL3.
source: We show that Pol IV's choice of initiating nucleotide, RDR2's initiation 1–2 nt internal to Pol IV transcript ends and RDR2's terminal transferase activity collectively yield a code that influences which precursor end is diced and whether 24 or 23 nt siRNAs are produced.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: RDR2 initiates transcription 1–2 nt internal to Pol IV transcript ends.
source: We show that Pol IV's choice of initiating nucleotide, RDR2's initiation 1–2 nt internal to Pol IV transcript ends and RDR2's terminal transferase activity collectively yield a code that influences which precursor end is diced and whether 24 or 23 nt siRNAs are produced.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: RDR2's terminal transferase activity influences whether 24 or 23 nt siRNAs are produced.
source: We show that Pol IV's choice of initiating nucleotide, RDR2's initiation 1–2 nt internal to Pol IV transcript ends and RDR2's terminal transferase activity collectively yield a code that influences which precursor end is diced and whether 24 or 23 nt siRNAs are produced.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and prior studies on RDR2's terminal transferase activity.

claim: Alternative patterns of DCL3 dicing allow for maximal siRNA coverage at methylated target loci by diversifying the size, sequence, and strand specificity of siRNAs.
source: By diversifying the size, sequence, and strand specificity of siRNAs derived from a given precursor, alternative patterns of DCL3 dicing allow for maximal siRNA coverage at methylated target loci.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and supported by inference from the data.

claim: Plant siRNAs range in size from 21 to 24 nt.
source: Plant siRNAs range in size from 21 to 24 nt, with DCL3-dependent 23 and 24 nt siRNAs (Xie et al., 2004; Henderson et al., 2006) accounting for ~90% of the total siRNA pool (Kasschau et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2007; Mosher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: DCL3-dependent 23 and 24 nt siRNAs account for ~90% of the total siRNA pool.
source: Plant siRNAs range in size from 21 to 24 nt, with DCL3-dependent 23 and 24 nt siRNAs (Xie et al., 2004; Henderson et al., 2006) accounting for ~90% of the total siRNA pool (Kasschau et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2007; Mosher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: 24 nt siRNAs stably associate with ARGONAUTE 4 (AGO4).
source: The 24 nt siRNAs stably associate with one of several Argonaute family proteins, primarily ARGONAUTE 4 (AGO4) (Zilberman et al., 2003; Qi et al., 2006), and guide resulting complexes to target loci via base-pairing interactions with long noncoding RNAs synthesized by multisubunit NUCLEAR RNA POLYMERASE V (Figure 1A; Wierzbicki et al., 2008; Wierzbicki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: AGO4-siRNA complexes are guided to target loci via base-pairing interactions with long noncoding RNAs synthesized by NUCLEAR RNA POLYMERASE V.
source: The 24 nt siRNAs stably associate with one of several Argonaute family proteins, primarily ARGONAUTE 4 (AGO4) (Zilberman et al., 2003; Qi et al., 2006), and guide resulting complexes to target loci via base-pairing interactions with long noncoding RNAs synthesized by multisubunit NUCLEAR RNA POLYMERASE V (Figure 1A; Wierzbicki et al., 2008; Wierzbicki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Protein-protein interactions between AGO4 and the C-terminal domain of the Pol V largest subunit contribute to AGO4 localization at target loci.
source: Protein-protein interactions between AGO4 and the C-terminal domain of the Pol V largest subunit, or Pol V-associated protein SPT5L, also contribute to AGO4 localization at target loci (El-Shami et al., 2007; He et al., 2009; Lahmy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Protein-protein interactions between AGO4 and Pol V-associated protein SPT5L contribute to AGO4 localization at target loci.
source: Protein-protein interactions between AGO4 and the C-terminal domain of the Pol V largest subunit, or Pol V-associated protein SPT5L, also contribute to AGO4 localization at target loci (El-Shami et al., 2007; He et al., 2009; Lahmy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: AGO4 localization at target loci leads to recruitment of the de novo DNA methyltransferase DRM2.
source: Subsequent recruitment of the de novo DNA methyltransferase, DRM2 (Cao and Jacobsen, 2002; Zhong et al., 2014) and other chromatin modifying enzymes then leads to the establishment of repressive chromatin environments that inhibit promoter-dependent transcription by DNA-dependent RNA Polymerases I, II, or III (Matzke and Mosher, 2014; Wendte and Pikaard, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RNA-directed DNA methylation establishes repressive chromatin environments that inhibit promoter-dependent transcription by DNA-dependent RNA Polymerases I, II, or III.
source: Subsequent recruitment of the de novo DNA methyltransferase, DRM2 (Cao and Jacobsen, 2002; Zhong et al., 2014) and other chromatin modifying enzymes then leads to the establishment of repressive chromatin environments that inhibit promoter-dependent transcription by DNA-dependent RNA Polymerases I, II, or III (Matzke and Mosher, 2014; Wendte and Pikaard, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RNA-directed DNA methylation facilitates transcriptional silencing at thousands of loci throughout plant genomes.
source: In this way, RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM) facilitates transcriptional silencing at thousands of loci throughout plant genomes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact supported by the broader context of the manuscript and citations.

claim: Pol IV associates with RDR2 via direct physical interaction.
source: Pol IV associates with RDR2 (Law et al., 2011; Haag et al., 2012) via direct physical interaction (Mishra et al., 2021) to form a multi-functional enzyme complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The transcription reactions of Pol IV and RDR2 are tightly coupled.
source: The transcription reactions of Pol IV and RDR2 are tightly coupled (Singh et al., 2019) with Pol IV's inability to maintain processivity through double-stranded DNA regions proposed to results in Pol IV arrest and backtracking, coincident with DNA template-nontemplate strand reannealing and extrusion of the nascent transcript's 3′ end for engagement by RDR2 (Fukudome et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pol IV-RDR2 dsRNAs range in size from ~25 to 40 bp in vivo.
source: Resulting double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs), ranging in size from ~25 to 40 bp in vivo (Blevins et al., 2015; Zhai et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2016) are then diced by DCL3.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Biogenesis of 23 and 24 nt siRNAs can be recapitulated in vitro upon incubating purified Pol IV, RDR2, and DCL3 with single-stranded bacteriophage M13 template DNA and nucleoside triphosphates.
source: Biogenesis of 23 and 24 nt siRNAs can be recapitulated in vitro upon incubating purified Pol IV, RDR2, and DCL3 with single-stranded bacteriophage M13 template DNA and nucleoside triphosphates, indicating that no other activities are needed (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Immunoprecipitated AGO4 associates almost entirely with 24 nt siRNAs.
source: Although DCL3 generates both 23 and 24 nt siRNAs, immunoprecipitated AGO4 associates almost entirely with 24 nt siRNAs (Mi et al., 2008; Havecker et al., 2010), making the significance of 23 nt siRNAs unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 23 nt siRNAs help specify the stable AGO4-association of 24 nt siRNAs when paired with them.
source: We have proposed that when paired with 24 nt siRNAs, the 23 nt RNAs help specify the stable AGO4-association of the 24 nt strands (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their prior work.

claim: An untemplated nucleotide is often present at the 3′ ends of RDR2 transcripts.
source: An untemplated nucleotide is often present at the 3′ ends of RDR2 transcripts and is enriched among 23 nt, but not 24 nt siRNAs (Singh and Pikaard, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: The untemplated nucleotide at the 3′ end of RDR2 transcripts is enriched among 23 nt siRNAs but not 24 nt siRNAs.
source: An untemplated nucleotide is often present at the 3′ ends of RDR2 transcripts and is enriched among 23 nt, but not 24 nt siRNAs (Singh and Pikaard, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: RDR2's terminal transferase activity can account for the addition of untemplated 3′ terminal nucleotides.
source: RDR2's terminal transferase activity can account for the addition of these untemplated 3′ terminal nucleotides (Blevins et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: DCL3 cuts a 37/38 nt dsRNA with a 1 nt 3′ overhang to yield 23 and 24 nt products.
source: DCL3 cuts the 37/38 nt dsRNA to yield 23 and 24 nt products (Figure 1C, lanes 1 and 5) as predicted by the model.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C.

claim: DCL3 cuts a dsRNA with a 2 nt overhang, formed by annealing 37 and 39 nt RNAs, generating two 24 nt RNAs.
source: Similarly, DCL3 cuts a dsRNA with a 2 nt overhang, formed by annealing 37 and 39 nt RNAs, generating two 24 nt RNAs (Figure 1C, lanes 2 and 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C.

claim: DCL3 measures and cuts 24 nt from the 5′ end of the top strand and makes an offset cut of the bottom strand to leave a 2 nt 3′ overhang.
source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that DCL3 measures and cuts 24 nt from the 5′ end of the top strand, and makes an offset cut of the bottom strand to leave a 2 nt 3′ overhang, as expected from prior studies (Zhang et al., 2004; Takeshita et al., 2007; Nagano et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C and citations to prior research.

claim: The length of the bottom strand of a dsRNA substrate can vary, indicating that its 3′ end is not anchored at a fixed position within DCL3.
source: The results also suggest that the length of the bottom strand can vary, indicating that its 3′ end is not anchored at a fixed position within DCL3.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 1C.

claim: Given a dsRNA substrate with two blunt ends, DCL3 generates dicing products of diverse sizes, including 21, 22, 24, and 25 nt RNAs.
source: Given a dsRNA substrate with two blunt ends, DCL3 generates dicing products of diverse sizes, including 21, 22, 24, and 25 nt RNAs (Figure 1C, compare lanes 3 and 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C.

claim: 21, 22, and 25 nt dicing products are not observed at significant levels among siRNAs produced in vitro by Pol IV, RDR2, and DCL3.
source: Importantly, 21, 22, and 25 nt dicing products are not observed at significant levels among siRNAs produced in vitro by Pol IV, RDR2, and DCL3 (Singh et al., 2019), nor have RNAs of these sizes been attributed to DCL3 activity based on analysis of dcl3 mutants in vivo (Xie et al., 2004; Henderson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RNAs of 21, 22, and 25 nt have not been attributed to DCL3 activity based on analysis of dcl3 mutants in vivo.
source: Importantly, 21, 22, and 25 nt dicing products are not observed at significant levels among siRNAs produced in vitro by Pol IV, RDR2, and DCL3 (Singh et al., 2019), nor have RNAs of these sizes been attributed to DCL3 activity based on analysis of dcl3 mutants in vivo (Xie et al., 2004; Henderson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: dsRNAs with 3′ overhangs, not blunt ends, best account for the 23 and 24 nt siRNAs generated by DCL3.
source: These considerations, combined with the results of Figure 1C, indicate that dsRNAs with 3′ overhangs, not blunt ends, best account for the 23 and 24 nt siRNAs generated by DCL3.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and prior knowledge.

claim: DCL3 prefers 3′ overhanging ends over blunt ends.
source: Collectively, the results of Figure 1 show that DCL3 will cut dsRNAs with 3′ overhanging ends or blunt ends but prefers 3′ overhanging ends.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: When DCL3 dices a dsRNA with a 3′ overhang on the left side and a blunt end on the right side, it preferentially dices from the 3′ overhanging end.
source: If the 3′ overhanging end is preferred by DCL3, a 24 nt 32P-labeled dicing product is expected from the 32P-labeled top strand and a 16 nt product is expected from the 32P-labeled bottom strand. This is observed, with dsRNA substrates that have 3′ overhangs of 1 or 2 nt yielding nearly identical products (Figure 1D, compare lanes 1–4 to lanes 5–8) and reaction time-courses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 – (B)).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1D.

claim: If DCL3 is incubated with a dsRNA with two blunt ends, DCL3 dices from both ends.
source: In contrast, if DCL3 is incubated with a dsRNA with two blunt ends, DCL3 dices from both ends, generating 16 and 24 nt products from both strands (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1E.

claim: DCL3 measures only one strand of its dsRNA substrates.
source: Experiments testing the dicing of dsRNAs formed by annealing RNA strands ranging in size from 22 to 25 nt yielded additional evidence that DCL3 measures only one strand of its dsRNA substrates (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2.

claim: Using a 24/25 nt duplex with a 1 nt 3′ overhang, the 24 nt top strand was not cut by DCL3, but the bottom strand was trimmed by 2 nt to yield a 23 nt product.
source: Using a duplex whose top strand was 24 nt and whose bottom strand was 25 nt, thus generating a 1 nt 3′ overhang on the left side, the 24 nt top strand was not cut by DCL3, but the bottom strand was trimmed by 2 nt to yield a 23 nt product (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2A.

claim: Dicing of a 24/24 nt dsRNA with two blunt ends by DCL3 occurs from the left or right sides, with one 24 nt strand uncut and the paired strand trimmed to 22 nt RNA.
source: We next tested a duplex with two blunt ends, formed by annealing two 24 nt RNAs (Figure 2B; note that these 24 nt RNAs have different gel mobilities). Dicing by DCL3 occurred from the left or right sides, due to the absence of a 3′ overhang to bias dicing to one side. In each case, one 24 nt strand was uncut whereas the paired strand was trimmed to 22 nt RNA (Figure 2B, lane 3; note that the alternative 22 nt RNAs also have different gel mobilities).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2B.

claim: DCL3's measurement of an interval equivalent to 24 nt is a consequence of interaction with the recessed 5′ end of the top strand.
source: This indicates that DCL3's measurement of an interval equivalent to 24 nt is a consequence of interaction with the recessed 5′ end of the top strand.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 2B.

claim: The bottom strand of a dsRNA substrate is cut by DCL3 at a position offset by 2 nt from where the 24th nucleotide would have been present in the top strand.
source: The bottom strand was cut at a position offset by 2 nt from where the 24th nucleotide would have been present in the top strand had the top strand been long enough.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 2B.

claim: DCL3 does not cut either strand of a 24/23 nt duplex with a 1 nt 3′ overhang on the left side and a 2 nt 3′ overhang on the right side.
source: Next, we annealed a 24 nt top strand and a 23 nt bottom strand to generate a duplex with a 1 nt 3′ overhang on the left side and a 2 nt 3′ overhang on the right side (Figure 2C), which mimics the dicing product proposed in Figure 1B (and Singh et al., 2019) and verified in Figure 1C. DCL3 does not cut either stand of this duplex RNA (Figure 2C, compare lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2C.

claim: The asymmetric 24/23 nt dsRNA duplex fits into DCL3 with the RNase domains aligned with the pre-existing ends of the RNA strands, resulting in no cutting.
source: This suggests that the asymmetric 24/23 nt dsRNA duplex fits into the enzyme with the RNase domains aligned with the pre-existing ends of the RNA strands. As a result, no cutting occurs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 2C.

claim: A 24/24 nt duplex having 2 nt 3′ overhangs at both ends was not cut by DCL3.
source: A 24/24 nt duplex having 2 nt 3′ overhangs at both ends was also not cut by DCL3 (Figure 2C, compare lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2C.

claim: DCL3 dicing products are not substrates for further dicing.
source: These results indicate that DCL3 dicing products are not substrates for further dicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 2C.

claim: Duplexes formed by annealing 23 and 22 nt RNA strands yield a ladder of digestion products as short as 17 nt when diced by DCL3.
source: Unlike 24/23 and 24/24 dicing products that are not diced further, duplexes formed by annealing 23 and 22 nt RNA strands, in various permutations, yielded a ladder of digestion products as short as 17 nt (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2D.

claim: dsRNAs whose strands are shorter than typical DCL3 dicing products do not fit into the enzyme in a way that fixes their position, allowing for cutting at variable positions.
source: This suggests that dsRNAs whose strands are shorter than typical DCL3 dicing products do not fit into the enzyme in a way that fixes their position, allowing for cutting at variable positions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 2D.

claim: DCL3 could play a role in the cleavage and turnover of dsRNAs smaller than its dicing products in vivo.
source: The results also raise the possibility that DCL3 could play a role in the cleavage and turnover of dsRNAs smaller than its dicing products in vivo.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental results in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutating both RNase III domains of DCL3 abolishes dicing.
source: Mutating both RNase III domains abolished dicing (compare lanes 5 and 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutating RNase III domain A of DCL3, while leaving domain B unchanged, results in top strand cutting to 24 nt, but no bottom strand cutting.
source: Mutating RNase III domain A, while leaving domain B unchanged, resulted in top strand (26 nt) cutting to 24 nt, but no bottom strand (27 nt) cutting (lane 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutating RNase III domain B of DCL3, but leaving domain A unchanged, allows bottom strand cutting to 23 nt.
source: Conversely, mutating domain B, but leaving domain A unchanged, allowed bottom strand cutting, to 23 nt (lane 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B.

claim: The PAZ domain of DCL3 binds the recessed 5′ end of the top RNA strand and cuts that strand using RNase III domain B at a distance equivalent to 24 nt.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the PAZ domain binds the recessed 5′ end of the top RNA strand, opposite the 3′ overhang of the bottom strand, and cuts that strand using RNase III domain B at a distance equivalent to 24 nt.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 3B and 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The paired strand of a dsRNA substrate is cut by RNase III domain A of DCL3, with the 3′ overhanging end of this strand not anchored at a fixed distance, allowing its diced products to vary in length.
source: The paired strand is cut by RNase III domain A, with the 3′ overhanging end of this strand not anchored at a fixed distance, allowing its diced products to vary in length (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 3B and 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DCL3 cleaves dsRNA substrates whose top strands begin with 5′ A or U more efficiently than those beginning with C or G.
source: This experiment revealed that DCL3 cleaves dsRNA substrates whose top strands begin with 5′ A or U (lanes 5–10) more efficiently than those beginning with C or G (lanes 11–16), in agreement with prior results comparing cell-free lysates of wild-type and dcl3 mutant plants (Nagano et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4A and supported by citation.

claim: An AU or UA pair is preferred over a GC or CG pair at the precursor's terminus for DCL3 dicing.
source: The fact that A or U allows for similar dicing efficiency suggests that an AU or UA pair is preferred over a GC or CG pair at the precursor's terminus.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 4A.

claim: No significant difference in DCL3 cleavage efficiency was observed for bottom strands having A, U, C, or G as the overhanging nucleotide.
source: We next tested whether DCL3 is affected by the nucleotide at the 3′ overhanging position of the bottom strand (Figure 4B). No significant difference in cleavage efficiency was observed for bottom strands having A, U, C, or G as the overhanging nucleotide, indicating that although the presence of 3′ overhang is important for dicing (Figure 1D), the identity of the overhanging nucleotide is unimportant.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4B.

claim: The presence of a 3′ overhang is important for DCL3 dicing, but the identity of the overhanging nucleotide is unimportant.
source: No significant difference in cleavage efficiency was observed for bottom strands having A, U, C, or G as the overhanging nucleotide, indicating that although the presence of 3′ overhang is important for dicing (Figure 1D), the identity of the overhanging nucleotide is unimportant.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 4B.

claim: The 5′ terminal nucleotide of a nascent RDR2 transcript is expected to possess a 5′ triphosphate group.
source: The 5′ terminal nucleotide of a nascent transcript is expected to possess a 5′ triphosphate group, and biochemical evidence indicates that this is true for RDR2 transcripts (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Pol IV-dependent transcripts generated in vivo or in vitro can be cloned via ligation reactions that require a 5′ monophosphate, without prior enzymatic treatments.
source: However, Pol IV-dependent transcripts generated in vivo or in vitro can be cloned via ligation reactions that require a 5′ monophosphate, without prior enzymatic treatments (Blevins et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015; Zhai et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2019), suggesting the possibility of an intrinsic or associated pyrophosphatase activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: If the bottom strand of a dsRNA substrate has a 5′ hydroxyl group, DCL3 preferentially engages the left side of the dsRNA substrate with a 5′ monophosphate and disfavors the right side with a 5′ hydroxyl.
source: This experiment revealed that if the bottom strand has a 5′ hydroxyl group, a strong 24 nt signal and weak 16 nt signal (barely above background levels) are observed (Figure 4C, lane 4). This indicates that DCL3 preferentially engaged the left side of the dsRNA substrate, which has a 5′ monophosphate, and disfavored the right side, which has a 5′ hydroxyl.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4C.

claim: If the bottom strand of a dsRNA substrate has a 5′ monophosphate or a triphosphate, more right-side dicing occurs, suggesting that monophosphates or triphosphates are similarly conducive to DCL3 engagement, but with monophosphates slightly preferred.
source: However, if the bottom strand also has a 5′ monophosphate (lane 5), or a triphosphate (lane 6), more right-side dicing occurs suggesting that monophosphates or triphosphates are similarly conducive to DCL3 engagement, but with monophosphates slightly preferred.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4C.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster Dicer-2 displays ATP-dependent activity for substrates with blunt-ends, but not overhanging ends.
source: Drosophila melanogaster Dicer-2 displays ATP-dependent activity for substrates with blunt-ends, but not overhanging ends (Sinha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Experiments comparing cell-free lysates of wild-type versus dcl3 mutant Arabidopsis plants suggested that binding, but not hydrolysis, of ATP is needed for DCL3 activity.
source: Moreover, experiments comparing cell-free lysates of wild-type versus dcl3 mutant Arabidopsis plants suggested that binding, but not hydrolysis, of ATP is needed for DCL3 activity (Nagano et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Arabidopsis DCL3 does not require ATP binding or hydrolysis for dicing.
source: In reactions containing 0 mM ATP, 5 mM ATP, or 5 mM ATP-γ-S, a non-hydrolyzable form of ATP, no requirement of ATP for DCL3 activity was observed, as monitored by the generation of labeled 24 nt dicing products (lanes 2–10 of Figure 5A, B; see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1). We conclude that Arabidopsis DCL3 does not require ATP binding or hydrolysis for dicing.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5A, 5B, and 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3′ overhangs are present at both termini of Pol IV-RDR2 transcribed dsRNAs.
source: Treatment of transcription reaction products with increasing amounts of S1 nuclease resulted in a progressive 1–2 nt shortening of labeled Pol IV transcripts (Figure 6B, lanes 1–4). Because the 32P label is at the 5′ end of these Pol IV transcripts, S1 trimming must be occurring at their 3′ ends. Body-labeled RDR2 transcripts were shortened by 1 nt upon digestion with S1 nuclease (Figure 6B, lanes 5–8), a result consistent with the removal of the single untemplated nucleotide added to the 3′ end of RDR2 transcripts. Collectively, the data of Figure 6B indicate that the 3′ ends of both the Pol IV transcripts and the RDR2 transcripts overhang the paired strand, fitting the predictions of the model in Figure 6A.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6B.

claim: RDR2 initiates transcription 1 or 2 nt internal to the 3′ ends of Pol IV transcripts.
source: S1 trimmed the 5′-labeled template strand of the RNA duplexes by 1–2 nt (lanes 1 and 2). As controls, we synthesized RNA strands with perfect complementarity to the template strand (lanes 3 and 4) or were shorter by 1 (lanes 5 and 6) or 2 nt (lanes 7 and 8) at their 5′ ends, annealed these RNAs to the 5′ end-labeled template RNA strand, and subjected resulting dsRNAs to S1 nuclease digestion. S1 digestion patterns for synthetic dsRNAs with 1 or 2 nt overhangs most closely resembled the digestion patterns observed for RDR2 transcription products (compare lanes 2, 6, and 8). We conclude that RDR2 initiates transcription 1 or 2o nt internal to the 3′ ends of the Pol IV transcripts it uses as templates, consistent with the results of Figure 6B, scenarios 2 and 3 of Figure 6A, and the results of a different assay (Fukudome et al., 2021).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6C and supported by citation.

claim: 24 nt siRNAs come from the 5′ ends of Pol IV transcripts and the 5′ ends of RDR2 transcripts.
source: Collectively, the experiments of Figure 6D reveal that the siRNAs derived from the 5′ ends of Pol IV transcripts and the 5′ ends of RDR2 transcripts are 24 nt, consistent with DCL3 measuring and cutting 24 nt from the 5′ end of either strand.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6D.

claim: 23 nt siRNAs come from the 3′ ends of Pol IV and RDR2 transcripts.
source: We thus deduce that the 23 nt siRNA dicing products, which are observed only when Pol IV or RDR2 transcripts are body-labeled (lanes 4 and 6), come from the 3′ ends of Pol IV and RDR2 transcripts.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 6D.

claim: Pol IV acts first in siRNA biogenesis, transcribing single-stranded template DNA to generate RNA transcripts whose 5′ to 3′ polarity is opposite that of the DNA.
source: These experiments showed definitively that Pol IV acts first, transcribing the single-stranded template DNA to generate RNA transcripts whose 5′ to 3′ polarity is opposite that of the DNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: RDR2 acts second in siRNA biogenesis, using the Pol IV transcripts as templates to generate complementary RNAs that are oriented in the same 5′ to 3′ polarity as the DNA template strand.
source: RDR2 acts second, using the Pol IV transcripts as templates to generate complementary RNAs that are oriented in the same 5′ to 3′ polarity as the DNA template strand, and thus could not have been directly transcribed from the DNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: 24 and 23 nt siRNAs are generated from both the Pol IV and the RDR2-transcribed strands of siRNA precursors.
source: These studies showed that 24 and 23 nt siRNAs are generated from both the Pol IV and the RDR2-transcribed strands of siRNA precursors, with 24 nt siRNAs outnumbering 23 nt siRNAs by several fold (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: 24 nt siRNAs outnumber 23 nt siRNAs by several fold.
source: These studies showed that 24 and 23 nt siRNAs are generated from both the Pol IV and the RDR2-transcribed strands of siRNA precursors, with 24 nt siRNAs outnumbering 23 nt siRNAs by several fold (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: An untemplated nucleotide at the 3′ terminus is a characteristic of RDR2 transcripts, but not Pol IV transcripts.
source: Moreover, these studies showed that an untemplated nucleotide at the 3′ terminus is a characteristic of RDR2 transcripts, but not Pol IV transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: The untemplated 3′-terminal nucleotide persists in siRNAs derived from RDR2 transcripts and is selectively enriched among 23 nt siRNAs but not 24 nt siRNAs.
source: The untemplated 3′-terminal nucleotide persists in siRNAs derived from RDR2 transcripts and, importantly, is selectively enriched among 23 nt siRNAs but not 24 nt siRNAs (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: 23 nt siRNAs also come from the 3′ ends of Pol IV transcripts.
source: However, 23 nt siRNAs also come from the 3′ ends of Pol IV transcripts (Figure 6D), helping explain why not all 23 nt siRNAs possess an untemplated nucleotide (Wang et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6D and supported by citations.

claim: Not all 23 nt siRNAs possess an untemplated nucleotide.
source: However, 23 nt siRNAs also come from the 3′ ends of Pol IV transcripts (Figure 6D), helping explain why not all 23 nt siRNAs possess an untemplated nucleotide (Wang et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: If Pol IV initiates with an adenosine, left-side dicing is favored, with DCL3 generating a diced duplex consisting of a 24 nt siRNA from the 5′ end of the Pol IV strand paired with a 23 nt siRNA from the 3′ end of the RDR2 strand.
source: Collectively, our experiments suggest that if Pol IV initiates with an adenosine, left-side dicing is favored, with DCL3 generating a diced duplex consisting of a 24 nt siRNA from the 5′ end of the Pol IV strand paired with a 23 nt siRNA from the 3′ end of the RDR2 strand (Figure 7, dicing scenario 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: If Pol IV transcription begins with a G, this encourages right-side dicing, especially if the RDR2 strand has a 5′ A or U that is optimal for DCL3 engagement.
source: By contrast, if Pol IV transcription begins with a G, we propose that this encourages right-side dicing, especially if the RDR2 strand has a 5′ A or U that is optimal for DCL3 engagement.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental results.

claim: RDR2 transcripts initiate most frequently with A or U.
source: Indeed, RNA-seq data have shown that RDR2 transcripts initiate most frequently with A or U (Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Consensus sequences of in vivo precursor 5′ and 3′ ends best matched consensus sequences for siRNA 5′ and 3′ ends by invoking left-side dicing for precursors that initiated with A and right-side dicing for precursors that initiated with G.
source: Moreover, consensus sequences of in vivo precursor 5′ and 3′ ends best matched consensus sequences for siRNA 5′ and 3′ ends by invoking left-side dicing for precursors that initiated with A and right-side dicing for precursors that initiated with G (Blevins et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Right-side dicing accounts for 24 nt siRNAs derived from the RDR2 strand and 23 nt siRNAs derived from the Pol IV strand.
source: Our current study shows that it is this right-side dicing that accounts for 24 nt siRNAs derived from the RDR2 strand and 23 nt siRNAs derived from the Pol IV strand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: There are two ways to generate 24 nt siRNAs from each strand and only one way to generate 23 nt siRNAs from each strand.
source: There are two ways to generate 24 nt siRNAs from each strand and only one way to generate 23 nt siRNAs from each strand (Figures 6A and 7), which fits with the fact that 24 nt siRNAs are more abundant than 23 nt siRNAs, both in vivo and in vitro (Blevins et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the models in Figures 6A and 7 and supported by citations.

claim: Pol IV transcripts that are 24 nt or longer are sufficient to give rise to DCL3-dependent siRNAs.
source: Our study also provides new insight into the minimum length of Pol IV or RDR2 transcripts that can serve as siRNA precursors or siRNAs. The experiments of Figure 2 indicate that Pol IV transcripts that are 24 nt or longer are sufficient to give rise to DCL3-dependent siRNAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2.

claim: If Pol IV generates a 24 nt transcript and RDR2 initiates 2 nt internal to this transcript and adds an extra untemplated nucleotide to the 3′ end of its transcript, the result would be a 24/23 nt dsRNA duplex that would not need to be diced by DCL3.
source: Moreover, if Pol IV were to generate a 24 nt transcript and RDR2 were to initiate 2 nt internal to this transcript and add an extra untemplated nucleotide to the 3′ end of its transcript, the result would be a 24/23 nt dsRNA duplex. This duplex would not need to be diced by DCL3 because it is already indistinguishable from a dicing product (see Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 2C.

claim: In dcl2 dcl3 dcl4 triple mutants, Pol IV-dependent 24 nt RNAs were detected at ~7% of the level found in wild-type plants.
source: Importantly, in dcl2 dcl3 dcl4 triple mutants, we detected Pol IV-dependent 24 nt RNAs at ~7% of the level found in wild-type plants (Blevins et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Low levels of RNA-directed DNA methylation persist in dicer mutants, which may be accounted for by Pol IV-dependent 24 nt RNAs that do not require dicing.
source: This may account for low levels of RNA-directed DNA methylation that persist in dicer mutants, suggesting an alternative explanation to putative dicer-independent pathways that have been proposed to be distinct from the canonical RNA-directed DNA methylation pathway yet remain unidentified (Yang et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: 24 nt siRNAs associated with AGO4 tend to begin with a 5′ adenosine.
source: Another prior finding in need of reconsideration is the observation that 24 nt siRNAs associated with AGO4 tend to begin with a 5′ adenosine (Mi et al., 2008), a finding that has been interpreted as evidence that AGO4 actively selects siRNAs that begin with an adenosine.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Pol IV and RDR2 transcripts most frequently begin with adenosine.
source: We have shown that Pol IV and RDR2 transcripts most frequently begin with adenosine (Singh et al., 2019) and our current study shows that DCL3 preferentially dices substrates with A at their 5′ ends.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: DCL3 preferentially dices substrates with A at their 5′ ends.
source: We have shown that Pol IV and RDR2 transcripts most frequently begin with adenosine (Singh et al., 2019) and our current study shows that DCL3 preferentially dices substrates with A at their 5′ ends.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4A.

claim: Pol IV, RDR2, and DCL3 activities could collectively account for much of the 5′ A-enrichment among siRNAs that become loaded into AGO4.
source: Thus Pol IV, RDR2, and DCL3 activities could collectively account for much of the 5′ A-enrichment among siRNAs that become loaded into AGO4.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and prior findings.

claim: 24 nt RNAs that have a 5′ A, U, C, or G are assimilated into AGO4 with similar efficiency in vitro.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, 24 nt RNAs that have a 5′ A, U, C, or G are assimilated into AGO4 with similar efficiency in vitro (Wang and Pikaard, unpublished).
evidence: This is unpublished data from the authors.

claim: DCL3 measures a fixed length of RNA equivalent to 24 nt, corresponding to the distance from a phosphorylated or triphosphorylated 5′ terminal nucleotide bound by the PAZ domain to the RNase III domain B cleavage site.
source: This fixed length presumably corresponds to the distance from a phosphorylated or triphosphorylated 5′ terminal nucleotide, bound by the PAZ domain, as in other Dicers (Park et al., 2011; Tian et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2018), to the RNase III domain B cleavage site of DCL3, a length equivalent to 24 nt.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to prior research on other Dicers.

claim: The siRNAs of alternative size (23 nt) come from the opposite strand of RNA, with the 5′ end generated by the RNase III domain A cleavage reaction.
source: The siRNAs of alternative size (23 nt) come from the opposite strand of RNA. The 5′ end of the non-measured strand is generated by the RNase III domain A cleavage reaction, but the 3′ end of this strand is apparently not anchored at a set distance, unlike human dicer (Park et al., 2011), and can overhang the 5′ end of the measured strand by 1 nt, to yield a 23 nt siRNA, or 2 nt to yield a 24 nt siRNA (see Figures 6A and 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation.

claim: The 3′ end of the non-measured strand is apparently not anchored at a set distance in DCL3, unlike human dicer.
source: The 5′ end of the non-measured strand is generated by the RNase III domain A cleavage reaction, but the 3′ end of this strand is apparently not anchored at a set distance, unlike human dicer (Park et al., 2011), and can overhang the 5′ end of the measured strand by 1 nt, to yield a 23 nt siRNA, or 2 nt to yield a 24 nt siRNA (see Figures 6A and 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation.

claim: A structural study of DCL3 bound to dsRNA supports the interpretation that the 3′ end of the non-measured strand is not anchored at a fixed distance.
source: A structural study of DCL3 bound to dsRNA, published while our study was in review, supports this interpretation (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent structural study.

claim: Pol IV and RDR2 physically interact.
source: Pol IV and RDR2 physically interact (Mishra et al., 2021) and their activities are tightly coupled such that Pol IV transcripts are channeled directly to RDR2 (Singh et al., 2019) by a proposed mechanism involving Pol IV backtracking (Fukudome et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pol IV transcripts are channeled directly to RDR2.
source: Pol IV and RDR2 physically interact (Mishra et al., 2021) and their activities are tightly coupled such that Pol IV transcripts are channeled directly to RDR2 (Singh et al., 2019) by a proposed mechanism involving Pol IV backtracking (Fukudome et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lack of Pol IV-interaction explains why the other five RNA-dependent RNA polymerases in Arabidopsis thaliana are not redundant with RDR2.
source: Lack of Pol IV-interaction explains why the other five RNA-dependent RNA polymerases in Arabidopsis thaliana are not redundant with RDR2.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Idiosyncrasies of Pol IV and RDR2 transcription inform DCL3 how to dice the dsRNAs at the next step of the pathway.
source: Our current study now shows that idiosyncrasies of Pol IV and RDR2 transcription, including the choice of nucleotide used to initiate transcription, the alternative start site positions of RDR2 internal to Pol IV transcripts, and the non-templated addition of a nucleotide at the 3′ end of RDR2 transcripts, collectively inform DCL3 how to dice the dsRNAs at the next step of the pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The specification of 23 and 24 nt siRNAs has functional significance, by specifying that the 24 nt RNA of a 23/24 nt RNA duplex becomes the siRNA stably associated with AGO4.
source: Experimental evidence indicates that the specification of 23 and 24 nt siRNAs has functional significance, by specifying that the 24 nt RNA of a 23/24 nt RNA duplex becomes the siRNA stably associated with AGO4 (Wang and Pikaard, unpublished).
evidence: This is unpublished data from the authors.

claim: By generating 24 and 23 nt siRNAs from either strand and either end of the Pol IV-RDR2 dsRNAs, DCL3 can diversify the set of siRNAs that can be derived from short dsRNA precursors.
source: Thus, by generating 24 and 23 nt siRNAs from either strand and either end of the Pol IV-RDR2 dsRNAs, DCL3 can diversify the set of siRNAs that can be derived from short dsRNA precursors, enabling siRNA base-pairing with Pol V transcripts transcribed from either strand of target loci DNA to maximize DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Diversifying the siRNA pool enables siRNA base-pairing with Pol V transcripts transcribed from either strand of target loci DNA to maximize DNA methylation.
source: Thus, by generating 24 and 23 nt siRNAs from either strand and either end of the Pol IV-RDR2 dsRNAs, DCL3 can diversify the set of siRNAs that can be derived from short dsRNA precursors, enabling siRNA base-pairing with Pol V transcripts transcribed from either strand of target loci DNA to maximize DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Pol IV is a 12-subunit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that evolved as a specialized form of Pol II.
source: Biogenesis of siRNAs involved in RdDM begins with DNA transcription by Pol IV, a 12-subunit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that evolved as a specialized form of Pol II (Ream et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Pol IV's inability to maintain processivity through double-stranded DNA regions is proposed to result in Pol IV arrest and backtracking.
source: The transcription reactions of Pol IV and RDR2 are tightly coupled (Singh et al., 2019) with Pol IV's inability to maintain processivity through double-stranded DNA regions proposed to results in Pol IV arrest and backtracking, coincident with DNA template-nontemplate strand reannealing and extrusion of the nascent transcript's 3′ end for engagement by RDR2 (Fukudome et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.
